claim: Amphiphysin I is cleaved by asparagine endopeptidase (AEP) at N278 in the brains of AD patients.
source: Amphiphysin I is cleaved by a cysteine proteinase asparagine endopeptidase (AEP) at N278 in the brains of AD patients.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data showing the cleavage site (Figure 2a,b), Western blot analysis with anti-N278 antibody (Figure 2c), and immunohistochemistry of AD patient brains (Figure 2d).

claim: The amount of AEP-generated N-terminal fragment of Amphiphysin I (1-278) is increased with aging.
source: The amount of AEP-generated N-terminal fragment of Amphiphysin I (1-278) is increased with aging.
evidence: Western blot analysis shows age-dependent increase in Amphiphysin I (1-278) fragment in wild-type mice and Tau P301S mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a–d).

claim: Amphiphysin I (1-278) inhibits clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
source: Amphiphysin I (1-278) inhibits clathrin-mediated endocytosis and induces synaptic dysfunction.
evidence: Transferrin uptake assay shows decreased uptake in cells expressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) (Figure 3c,g), and FM 4-64 labeling shows reduced synaptic vesicle endocytosis (Figure 3e,i).

claim: Amphiphysin I (1-278) induces synaptic dysfunction.
source: Amphiphysin I (1-278) inhibits clathrin-mediated endocytosis and induces synaptic dysfunction.
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings show decreased mEPSC frequency in neurons expressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) (Figure 4a-c), and electron microscopy shows reduced synaptic density (Figure 6b,c).

claim: Amphiphysin I (1-278) binds p35 and promotes its transition to p25.
source: Furthermore, Amphiphysin I (1-278) binds p35 and promotes its transition to p25, thus activates CDK5 and enhances tau hyperphosphorylation.
evidence: His pull-down assay shows Amphiphysin I (1-278) binds to p35 (Figure 5j), and Western blot shows increased p25 in cytoplasm fraction in presence of Amphiphysin I (1-278) (Figure 5k).

claim: Amphiphysin I (1-278) activates CDK5.
source: Furthermore, Amphiphysin I (1-278) binds p35 and promotes its transition to p25, thus activates CDK5 and enhances tau hyperphosphorylation.
evidence: CDK5 activity assay shows increased kinase activity in neurons expressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) as measured by histone H1 phosphorylation (Figure 5a,d,e).

claim: Amphiphysin I (1-278) enhances tau hyperphosphorylation.
source: Furthermore, Amphiphysin I (1-278) binds p35 and promotes its transition to p25, thus activates CDK5 and enhances tau hyperphosphorylation.
evidence: Immunostaining shows increased AT8 and AT100 immunoreactivity in hippocampus sections overexpressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) (Figure 4d) and in cultured neurons (Figure 4e,f).

claim: Overexpression of Amphiphysin I (1-278) in the hippocampus of Tau P301S mice induces synaptic dysfunction.
source: Overexpression of Amphiphysin I (1-278) in the hippocampus of Tau P301S mice induces synaptic dysfunction, tau hyperphosphorylation, and cognitive deficits.
evidence: Electron microscopy shows reduced synaptic density (Figure 6b,c), Golgi staining shows loss of dendritic spines (Figure 6d,e), and electrophysiology shows diminished LTP (Figure 6k,l).

claim: Overexpression of Amphiphysin I (1-278) in the hippocampus of Tau P301S mice induces tau hyperphosphorylation.
source: Overexpression of Amphiphysin I (1-278) in the hippocampus of Tau P301S mice induces synaptic dysfunction, tau hyperphosphorylation, and cognitive deficits.
evidence: Immunohistochemistry shows increased AT8 and AT100 immunoreactivity in hippocampus of mice overexpressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) (Figure 4d).

claim: Overexpression of Amphiphysin I (1-278) in the hippocampus of Tau P301S mice induces cognitive deficits.
source: Overexpression of Amphiphysin I (1-278) in the hippocampus of Tau P301S mice induces synaptic dysfunction, tau hyperphosphorylation, and cognitive deficits.
evidence: Morris water maze test shows impaired learning ability and decreased time in target quadrant (Figure 6f-h), and Y-maze test shows less time in new arm (Figure 6j).

claim: Overexpression of the N278A mutant Amphiphysin I, which resists the AEP-mediated cleavage, alleviates the pathological and behavioral defects.
source: However, overexpression of the N278A mutant Amphiphysin I, which resists the AEP-mediated cleavage, alleviates the pathological and behavioral defects.
evidence: Electron microscopy shows higher synaptic density (Figure 7b,c), immunostaining shows decreased AT8 immunoreactivity (Figure 7d), water maze test shows improved memory (Figure 7e), and electrophysiology shows improved LTP (Figure 7f,g) in mice expressing N278A mutant.

claim: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common neurodegenerative disease.
source: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common neurodegenerative disease.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about AD prevalence.

claim: AD is characterized by the deposition of extracellular senile plaque and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs).
source: Pathologically, it is characterized by the deposition of extracellular senile plaque and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about AD pathology.

claim: Senile plaques are composed of amyloid-β (Aβ).
source: Senile plaques are composed of amyloid-β (Aβ), while NFTs are composed of hyperphosphorylated tau.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the composition of senile plaques.

claim: NFTs are composed of hyperphosphorylated tau.
source: Senile plaques are composed of amyloid-β (Aβ), while NFTs are composed of hyperphosphorylated tau.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the composition of NFTs.

claim: The extent of tau deposition is closely related to the severity of cognitive impairments.
source: The extent of tau deposition is closely related to the severity of cognitive impairments (Arriagada et al., 1992; Brier et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Tau is expressed in neurons and mainly distributed in axons.
source: Tau is expressed in neurons and mainly distributed in axons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tau localization.

claim: Tau acts as a microtubule-associated protein and regulates the dynamics of microtubules, mediating neuronal polarity, axonal outgrowth, and axonal transport.
source: It acts as a microtubule-associated protein and regulates the dynamics of microtubules, mediating neuronal polarity, axonal outgrowth, and axonal transport (Dixit et al., 2008; Harada et al., 1994; Tan et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: During the onset of AD, tau loses its physiological conformation and aggregates into amyloid fibrils.
source: During the onset of AD, tau loses its physiological conformation and aggregates into amyloid fibrils.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tau pathology in AD.

claim: Aggregated tau further recruits monomeric tau and propagates in a 'prion-like' manner.
source: Aggregated tau further recruits monomeric tau and propagates in a 'prion-like' manner (Frost et al., 2009; Clavaguera et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In the brain of AD patients, tau undergoes several posttranslational modifications including phosphorylation, truncation, acetylation, methylation, ubiquitylation, etc.
source: In the brain of AD patients, tau undergoes several posttranslational modifications including phosphorylation, truncation, acetylation, methylation, ubiquitylation, etc. (Cook et al., 2014; Pevalova et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Hyperphosphorylation is widely considered to be the major trigger that mediates tau pathology.
source: Hyperphosphorylation is widely considered to be the major trigger that mediates tau pathology.
evidence: This reflects established scientific consensus about tau pathology.

claim: Hyperphosphorylated tau loses its ability to associate with microtubules and is more prone to form paired helical filaments (PHFs).
source: Hyperphosphorylated tau loses its ability to associate with microtubules and is more prone to form paired helical filaments (PHFs) (Alonso et al., 2001; Alonso et al., 1996; Moszczynski et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Cyclin-dependent kinase 5 (CDK5) is a major kinase involved in the abnormal phosphorylation of tau in AD brains.
source: Cyclin-dependent kinase 5 (CDK5) is a major kinase involved in the abnormal phosphorylation of tau in AD brains (Engmann and Giese, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The kinase activity of CDK5 is regulated by its regulatory subunit p35.
source: The kinase activity of CDK5 is regulated by its regulatory subunit p35.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CDK5 regulation.

claim: P25, a truncated form of p35, is highly expressed in AD brains and constitutively activates CDK5.
source: P25, a truncated form of p35, is highly expressed in AD brains and constitutively activates CDK5 (Patrick et al., 1999; Seo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The activation of the p25/CDK5 pathway leads to the formation of neurofibrillary tangles and neurodegeneration.
source: Thus, the activation of the p25/CDK5 pathway leads to the formation of neurofibrillary tangles and neurodegeneration (Cruz et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The mechanisms that regulate the production of p25 and the activation of CDK5 in AD remain poorly understood.
source: But the mechanisms that regulate the production of p25 and the activation of CDK5 in AD remain poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Synaptic dysfunction is an early and invariant feature of AD, occurring long before the onset of cognitive symptoms.
source: In addition to the deposition of Aβ and tau, synaptic dysfunction is an early and invariant feature of AD, occurring long before the onset of cognitive symptoms.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AD pathology.

claim: The severity of dementia is correlated with the extent of synaptic loss.
source: The severity of dementia is correlated with the extent of synaptic loss (DeKosky and Scheff, 1990; Terry et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Both Aβ and tau contribute to synaptic dysfunction.
source: It has been demonstrated that both Aβ and tau contribute to synaptic dysfunction.
evidence: This is established knowledge based on previous research.

claim: Soluble Aβ oligomers induce synaptic dysfunction and block hippocampal long-term potentiation via binding to receptors on neurons.
source: Soluble Aβ oligomers induce synaptic dysfunction and block hippocampal long-term potentiation via binding to receptors on neurons (He et al., 2019; Laurén et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2013), while tau is required for Aβ-induced synaptic dysfunction (Ittner et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Tau is required for Aβ-induced synaptic dysfunction.
source: Soluble Aβ oligomers induce synaptic dysfunction and block hippocampal long-term potentiation via binding to receptors on neurons (He et al., 2019; Laurén et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2013), while tau is required for Aβ-induced synaptic dysfunction (Ittner et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Several synaptic proteins are decreased in the brain tissue of patients with AD.
source: Several synaptic proteins are decreased in the brain tissue of patients with AD, while the concentration of some synaptic proteins in the cerebral spinal fluids is increased, indicating synaptic degeneration (Bereczki et al., 2016; Bereczki et al., 2018; Kvartsberg et al., 2019; de Wilde et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The concentration of some synaptic proteins in the cerebral spinal fluids is increased in AD patients, indicating synaptic degeneration.
source: Several synaptic proteins are decreased in the brain tissue of patients with AD, while the concentration of some synaptic proteins in the cerebral spinal fluids is increased, indicating synaptic degeneration (Bereczki et al., 2016; Bereczki et al., 2018; Kvartsberg et al., 2019; de Wilde et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and includes an inference about synaptic degeneration.

claim: Amphiphysin I is a synaptic protein with an N-Bin/amphiphysin/Rvs (BAR) domain, which is involved in clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
source: Amphiphysin I is a synaptic protein with an N-Bin/amphiphysin/Rvs (BAR) domain, which is involved in clathrin-mediated endocytosis (Lichte et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: During the formation of newly retrieved presynaptic vesicles, Amphiphysin I senses and facilitates membrane curvature to mediate synaptic vesicles invagination and fission.
source: During the formation of newly retrieved presynaptic vesicles, Amphiphysin I senses and facilitates membrane curvature to mediate synaptic vesicles invagination and fission (Takei et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Amphiphysin I acts as a linker protein binding with dynamin, clathrin, Amphiphysin II, and other dephosphins in the clathrin-coated complex.
source: Amphiphysin I also acts as a linker protein binding with dynamin, clathrin, Amphiphysin II, and other dephosphins in the clathrin-coated complex (David et al., 1996; Takei et al., 1999; McMahon et al., 1997; Wigge et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Amphiphysin I interacts with CDK5 activator p35.
source: Besides, Amphiphysin I also interacts with CDK5 activator p35 (Floyd et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The expression of Amphiphysin I is reduced in brain regions with aggregates of hyperphosphorylated tau.
source: The expression of Amphiphysin I is reduced in brain regions with aggregates of hyperphosphorylated tau (De Jesús-Cortés et al., 2012), indicating dysfunction of Amphiphysin I is involved in the pathogenesis of AD.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Dysfunction of Amphiphysin I is involved in the pathogenesis of AD.
source: The expression of Amphiphysin I is reduced in brain regions with aggregates of hyperphosphorylated tau (De Jesús-Cortés et al., 2012), indicating dysfunction of Amphiphysin I is involved in the pathogenesis of AD.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of reduced Amphiphysin I expression in AD.

claim: The relationship between Amphiphysin I dysregulation and tau phosphorylation during the development of AD is unknown.
source: However, the relationship between Amphiphysin I dysregulation and tau phosphorylation during the development of AD is unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Asparagine endopeptidase (AEP) is a cysteine protease that specifically cleaves the peptide bonds on the C-terminal side of asparagine residues.
source: Asparagine endopeptidase (AEP) is a cysteine protease that specifically cleaves the peptide bonds on the C-terminal side of asparagine residues (Dall and Brandstetter, 2016; Chen et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: AEP is activated in the aging brain.
source: Recently, we showed that AEP is activated in the aging brain, cleaves amyloid precursor protein (APP) and tau, promoting the deposition of Aβ and tau in the brain (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research by the authors.

claim: AEP cleaves amyloid precursor protein (APP) and tau, promoting the deposition of Aβ and tau in the brain.
source: Recently, we showed that AEP is activated in the aging brain, cleaves amyloid precursor protein (APP) and tau, promoting the deposition of Aβ and tau in the brain (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research by the authors.

claim: AEP cleaves Amphiphysin I in vitro in a time-dependent manner.
source: Amphiphysin I was cleaved into two fragments in a time-dependent manner (Figure 1a).
evidence: Western blot data shows cleavage of Amphiphysin I by AEP at 5 and 10 min time points (Figure 1a).

claim: Purified Amphiphysin I is cleaved by active AEP enzyme.
source: Purified Amphiphysin I was also potently cleaved by active AEP enzyme (Figure 1b).
evidence: Western blot shows cleavage of purified GST-Amphiphysin I by recombinant AEP (Figure 1b).

claim: Wild-type AEP strongly induces Amphiphysin I fragmentation.
source: Wild-type AEP strongly induced Amphiphysin I fragmentation, while the AEP C189S mutant that abolishes its protease activity (Li et al., 2003) was unable to induce the cleavage of Amphiphysin I (Figure 1c).
evidence: Western blot shows cleavage of Amphiphysin I by wild-type AEP but not by C189S mutant (Figure 1c).

claim: The AEP C189S mutant that abolishes its protease activity is unable to induce the cleavage of Amphiphysin I.
source: Wild-type AEP strongly induced Amphiphysin I fragmentation, while the AEP C189S mutant that abolishes its protease activity (Li et al., 2003) was unable to induce the cleavage of Amphiphysin I (Figure 1c).
evidence: Western blot shows no cleavage of Amphiphysin I by C189S mutant AEP (Figure 1c), and the mutant's lack of activity is supported by citation.

claim: The AEP inhibitor AENK suppresses the cleavage of Amphiphysin I.
source: Moreover, the AEP inhibitor AENK suppressed the cleavage of Amphiphysin I, while its inactive analog AEQK did not affect this process (Figure 1d).
evidence: Western blot shows inhibition of Amphiphysin I cleavage by AENK but not AEQK (Figure 1d).

claim: The inactive analog AEQK does not affect the cleavage of Amphiphysin I by AEP.
source: Moreover, the AEP inhibitor AENK suppressed the cleavage of Amphiphysin I, while its inactive analog AEQK did not affect this process (Figure 1d).
evidence: Western blot shows no inhibition of Amphiphysin I cleavage by AEQK (Figure 1d).

claim: Amphiphysin I is a substrate of AEP.
source: Overall, these results indicate that Amphiphysin I is a substrate of AEP.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple in vitro cleavage experiments (Figure 1a-f).

claim: A (279-292) fragment of Amphiphysin I was found in wild-type mouse brain tissue lysate.
source: A (279-292) fragment of Amphiphysin I was found in wild-type mouse brain tissue lysate (Figure 2a).
evidence: Mass spectrometry analysis identified this fragment (Figure 2a).

claim: Comparative label-free proteomic analysis revealed greater than ninefold enrichment for the (279-292) fragment of Amphiphysin I in wild-type versus AEP–/– brain extracts.
source: Comparative label-free proteomic analysis against AEP–/– mice revealed greater than ninefold enrichment for this fragment in wild-type versus AEP–/– brain extracts, indicating Amphiphysin I is cleaved by AEP after N278 (Figure 2b).
evidence: Mass spectrometry data shows enrichment of the fragment in wild-type compared to AEP knockout mice (Figure 2b).

claim: N278 is the major AEP cleavage site on Amphiphysin I.
source: The mutation completely blocked the production of the strongest fragment (Figure 2c), confirming that N278 is the major AEP cleavage site on Amphiphysin I.
evidence: Western blot shows that N278A mutation prevents cleavage by AEP (Figure 2c).

claim: The expression of Amphiphysin I (1-278) fragment in AD brain tissues is higher than that in control brain tissues.
source: The expression of Amphiphysin I (1-278) fragment in AD brain tissues was higher than that in control brain tissues, as indicated by immunohistochemistry staining and Western blot (Figure 2d, Figure 2—figure supplement 2e–f).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry and Western blot show increased Amphiphysin I (1-278) in AD brains (Figure 2d, Figure 2—figure supplement 2e–f).

claim: Amphiphysin I (1-278) fragment colocalizes with AT8 staining.
source: Furthermore, we found that Amphiphysin I (1-278) fragment colocalized with AT8 staining (Figure 2e).
evidence: Co-immunostaining shows colocalization of anti-N278 with p-tau (AT8) in AD brain sections (Figure 2e).

claim: Amphiphysin I N278 fragment is present in the cortex and hippocampal CA1 region from the Tau P301S transgenic AD mouse model.
source: We also found the presence of Amphiphysin I N278 fragment in the cortex and hippocampal CA1 region from the Tau P301S transgenic AD mouse model, but few signals were found in the age-matched non-transgenic control brain sections (Figure 2f).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry shows Amphiphysin I N278 fragments in Tau P301S mice but not in wild-type mice (Figure 2f).

claim: Clathrin and dynamin I bind to full-length Amphiphysin I and Amphiphysin I (279-695) fragment.
source: Clathrin and dynamin I bound to full-length Amphiphysin I and Amphiphysin I (279-695) fragment, while Amphiphysin II bound to full-length Amphiphysin I and the (1-278) fragment (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: GST pull-down assay shows binding of clathrin and dynamin I to full-length and (279-695) fragment (Figure 3b).

claim: Amphiphysin II binds to full-length Amphiphysin I and the (1-278) fragment.
source: Clathrin and dynamin I bound to full-length Amphiphysin I and Amphiphysin I (279-695) fragment, while Amphiphysin II bound to full-length Amphiphysin I and the (1-278) fragment (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: GST pull-down assay shows binding of Amphiphysin II to full-length and (1-278) fragment (Figure 3b).

claim: Amphiphysin I fragments generated by AEP partially lose their activity to bind other endocytic proteins.
source: These results indicate that Amphiphysin I fragments generated by AEP partially lose their activity to bind other endocytic proteins, and may interfere with synaptic vesicles invagination and fission.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the GST pull-down data showing differential binding patterns (Figure 3b).

claim: Amphiphysin I fragments may interfere with synaptic vesicles invagination and fission.
source: These results indicate that Amphiphysin I fragments generated by AEP partially lose their activity to bind other endocytic proteins, and may interfere with synaptic vesicles invagination and fission.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed loss of binding activity.

claim: Transferrin uptake in cells transfected with Amphiphysin I (1-278) and Amphiphysin I (279-695) fragments is decreased by 25 and 22%, respectively, compared with cells expressing full-length Amphiphysin I.
source: Transferrin uptake assay found that transferrin uptake in cells transfected with Amphiphysin I (1-278) and Amphiphysin I (279-695) fragments was decreased by 25 and 22%, respectively, when compared with cells expressing full-length Amphiphysin I (Figure 3c,g).
evidence: Quantification of transferrin uptake shows decreased uptake in cells expressing fragments (Figure 3g).

claim: Overexpression of active AEP fragment (26-323) significantly inhibits transferrin uptake by 44%.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of active AEP fragment (26-323) also significantly inhibited transferrin uptake by 44% (Figure 3d,h).
evidence: Quantification of transferrin uptake shows decreased uptake in cells expressing active AEP (Figure 3h).

claim: FM 4–64 labeling in boutons expressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) or Amphiphysin I (279-695) is inhibited by 37 and 64%, respectively, compared with that in boutons expressing full-length Amphiphysin I.
source: FM 4–64 labeling in boutons expressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) or Amphiphysin I (279-695) was inhibited by 37 and 64%, respectively, compared with that in boutons expressing full-length Amphiphysin I (Figure 3e,i).
evidence: Quantification of FM 4-64 uptake shows decreased labeling in boutons expressing fragments (Figure 3i).

claim: The density of dendritic spines in neurons expressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) or Amphiphysin I (279-695) decreased by 36 and 18%, respectively, compared with that in neurons expressing full-length Amphiphysin I.
source: Besides, the density of dendritic spines in neurons expressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) or Amphiphysin I (279-695) decreased by 36 and 18%, respectively, compared with that in neurons expressing full-length Amphiphysin I (Figure 3f,j), indicating that Amphiphysin I fragments induce spine degeneration.
evidence: Quantification of dendritic spine density shows decreased density in neurons expressing fragments (Figure 3j).

claim: Amphiphysin I fragments induce spine degeneration.
source: Besides, the density of dendritic spines in neurons expressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) or Amphiphysin I (279-695) decreased by 36 and 18%, respectively, compared with that in neurons expressing full-length Amphiphysin I (Figure 3f,j), indicating that Amphiphysin I fragments induce spine degeneration.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed decrease in dendritic spine density.

claim: The Amphiphysin I fragments generated by AEP interfere with its function to interact with other dephosphins and impair the clathrin-mediated endocytosis and synaptic vesicle recycling.
source: All these results demonstrate that the Amphiphysin I fragments generated by AEP interfere with its function to interact with other dephosphins and impair the clathrin-mediated endocytosis and synaptic vesicle recycling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing impaired binding, transferrin uptake, FM 4-64 labeling, and spine density.

claim: The frequency but not the amplitude of mEPSCs is significantly decreased in neurons expressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) or Amphiphysin I (279-695) compared to neurons expressing full-length Amphiphysin I.
source: The frequency but not the amplitude of mEPSCs was significantly decreased in neurons expressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) or Amphiphysin I (279-695) than that in neurons expressing full-length Amphiphysin I (Figure 4b,c).
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings show decreased mEPSC frequency but not amplitude (Figure 4b,c).

claim: Amphiphysin I fragments interfere with synaptic transmission.
source: These results suggest that Amphiphysin I fragments interfere with synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed decrease in mEPSC frequency.

claim: There is a marked increase of AT8 and AT100 immunoreactivity in hippocampus sections overexpressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) compared with other groups.
source: Two months later, we found a marked increase of AT8 and AT100 immunoreactivity (Figure 4d) in hippocampus sections overexpressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) compared with other groups.
evidence: Immunostaining shows increased AT8 and AT100 in hippocampus overexpressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) (Figure 4d).

claim: Amphiphysin I (279-596) fragment slightly enhances tau phosphorylation compared with full-length Amphiphysin I.
source: Amphiphysin I (279-596) fragment also slightly enhanced tau phosphorylation compared with full-length Amphiphysin I (Figure 4d).
evidence: Immunostaining shows slightly increased tau phosphorylation with (279-596) fragment (Figure 4d).

claim: The levels of total tau are comparable among all groups overexpressing different Amphiphysin I constructs.
source: However, the levels of total tau were comparable among all groups, indicating that Amphiphysin I fragments promote tau phosphorylation but do not elevate the expression of total tau.
evidence: Immunostaining shows similar total tau levels across groups (Figure 4d).

claim: Amphiphysin I fragments promote tau phosphorylation but do not elevate the expression of total tau.
source: However, the levels of total tau were comparable among all groups, indicating that Amphiphysin I fragments promote tau phosphorylation but do not elevate the expression of total tau.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of increased phosphorylated tau but unchanged total tau levels.

claim: There is increased tau phosphorylation in neurons overexpressing Amphiphysin I fragments.
source: We further confirmed the effect of Amphiphysin I fragments on tau phosphorylation in cultured primary neurons. We found increased tau phosphorylation in neurons overexpressing Amphiphysin I fragments (Figure 4e,f).
evidence: Immunostaining of primary neurons shows increased AT8 and AT100 in neurons expressing fragments (Figure 4e,f).

claim: AT100 staining is mainly found in the nucleus.
source: The AT100 staining was mainly found in the nucleus, which is consistent with the previous reports (Gil et al., 2017; Hernández-Ortega et al., 2016, Gärtner et al., 1998).
evidence: This observation is supported by citations to previous reports.

claim: Amphiphysin I (1-278) enhances the phosphorylation of tau.
source: These in vivo and in vitro results indicate that Amphiphysin I (1-278) enhances the phosphorylation of tau.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments in mice and cultured neurons.

claim: CDK5 is one of the major kinases that induce the hyperphosphorylation of tau during AD pathology.
source: CDK5 is one of the major kinases that induce the hyperphosphorylation of tau during AD pathology (Zheng et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The activity of CDK5 in neurons expressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) is much higher than that in other groups.
source: We found that the activity of CDK5 in neurons expressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) was much higher than that in other groups (Figure 5d,e), indicating that Amphiphysin I (1-278) enhances the kinase activity of CDK5.
evidence: CDK5 activity assay shows increased phosphorylation of histone H1 in neurons expressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) (Figure 5d,e).

claim: Amphiphysin I (1-278) enhances the kinase activity of CDK5.
source: We found that the activity of CDK5 in neurons expressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) was much higher than that in other groups (Figure 5d,e), indicating that Amphiphysin I (1-278) enhances the kinase activity of CDK5.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed increase in CDK5 activity.

claim: The content of AT8 and AT100 is increased in neurons expressing Amphiphysin I (1-278).
source: Consistent with the increased CDK5 activity, the content of AT8 and AT100 was increased in neurons expressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) (Figure 5b,c).
evidence: Western blot shows increased AT8 and AT100 in neurons expressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) (Figure 5b,c).

claim: AT8 and AT100 immunoreactivity are significantly decreased in the presence of roscovitine in neurons overexpressing Amphiphysin I (1-278).
source: As expected, AT8 and AT100 immunoreactivity were significantly decreased in the presence of roscovitine (Figure 5f–h).
evidence: Immunostaining shows decreased AT8 and AT100 with CDK5 inhibitor treatment (Figure 5f-h).

claim: Amphiphysin I (1-278)-induced hyperphosphorylation of tau is mediated by CDK5.
source: To confirm whether Amphiphysin I (1-278)-induced hyperphosphorylation of tau is mediated by CDK5, we treated the neurons with 10 μM CDK5 inhibitor roscovitine in neurons overexpressing Amphiphysin I (1-278). As expected, AT8 and AT100 immunoreactivity were significantly decreased in the presence of roscovitine (Figure 5f–h).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that CDK5 inhibitor reduces tau phosphorylation induced by Amphiphysin I (1-278).

claim: There is increased p35 immunoreactivity in boutons overexpressing Amphiphysin I (1-278).
source: Interestingly, we observed increased p35 immunoreactivity in boutons overexpressing Amphiphysin I (1-278), suggesting that p35/p25 may mediate the effect of Amphiphysin I (1-278) on promoting CDK5 activity (Figure 5i).
evidence: Immunostaining shows increased p35 in boutons expressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) (Figure 5i).

claim: p35/p25 may mediate the effect of Amphiphysin I (1-278) on promoting CDK5 activity.
source: Interestingly, we observed increased p35 immunoreactivity in boutons overexpressing Amphiphysin I (1-278), suggesting that p35/p25 may mediate the effect of Amphiphysin I (1-278) on promoting CDK5 activity (Figure 5i).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed increase in p35 immunoreactivity.

claim: Amphiphysin I (1-278) fragment binds to p35.
source: We found that Amphiphysin I (1-278) fragment bound to p35, and enhanced the interaction between p35 and tau (Figure 5j).
evidence: His pull-down assay shows binding of Amphiphysin I (1-278) to p35 (Figure 5j).

claim: Amphiphysin I (1-278) fragment enhances the interaction between p35 and tau.
source: We found that Amphiphysin I (1-278) fragment bound to p35, and enhanced the interaction between p35 and tau (Figure 5j).
evidence: His pull-down assay shows enhanced interaction between p35 and tau in presence of Amphiphysin I (1-278) (Figure 5j).

claim: Amphiphysin I (1-278) fragment is more abundant in the cell membrane than full-length Amphiphysin I.
source: When GST-Amphiphysin I fragments and Flag-His-p35 were co-transfected into HEK293 cells, Amphiphysin I (1-278) fragment was more abundant in the cell membrane than full-length Amphiphysin I, while Amphiphysin I (279-695) fragment mainly distributed in the cytoplasm.
evidence: Western blot of cytoplasm and membrane fractions shows increased Amphiphysin I (1-278) in membrane (Figure 5k).

claim: Amphiphysin I (279-695) fragment mainly distributes in the cytoplasm.
source: When GST-Amphiphysin I fragments and Flag-His-p35 were co-transfected into HEK293 cells, Amphiphysin I (1-278) fragment was more abundant in the cell membrane than full-length Amphiphysin I, while Amphiphysin I (279-695) fragment mainly distributed in the cytoplasm.
evidence: Western blot of cytoplasm and membrane fractions shows Amphiphysin I (279-695) mainly in cytoplasm (Figure 5k).

claim: The expression of p25 is higher in the cytoplasm fraction in the presence of Amphiphysin I (1-278).
source: Furthermore, the expression of p25 was higher in the cytoplasm fraction in the presence of Amphiphysin I (1-278) (Figure 5k).
evidence: Western blot shows increased p25 in cytoplasm fraction with Amphiphysin I (1-278) (Figure 5k).

claim: Amphiphysin I (1-278) may sequester p35 in the membrane, where it is processed to p25 by calpain.
source: Thus, Amphiphysin I (1-278) may sequester p35 in the membrane, where it is processed to p25 by calpain (Minegishi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed membrane localization of Amphiphysin I (1-278) and increased p25, supported by citation about calpain processing of p35.

claim: Amphiphysin I (1-278) interacts with p35, activates CDK5, and induces the hyperphosphorylation of tau.
source: These results suggest that Amphiphysin I (1-278) interacts with p35, activates CDK5, and induces the hyperphosphorylation of tau.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing binding to p35, increased CDK5 activity, and increased tau phosphorylation.

claim: The Tau P301S mice express P301S mutant human tau and develop widespread neurofibrillary tangle-like inclusions in the brain.
source: The Tau P301S mice express P301S mutant human tau and develop widespread neurofibrillary tangle-like inclusions in the brain, which is accompanied by synaptic dysfunction and behavioral impairments (Yoshiyama et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The density of synapse in the hippocampus of mice injected with AAV-EGFP-Amphiphysin I fragments (1–278 and 279–695) is reduced compared to the mice overexpressing full-length Amphiphysin I.
source: Electron microscope analysis of brain sections showed that the density of synapse in the hippocampus of mice injected with AAV-EGFP-Amphiphysin I fragments (1–278 and 279–695) was reduced compared to the mice overexpressing full-length Amphiphysin I (Figure 6b,c).
evidence: Electron microscopy shows reduced synaptic density in mice expressing fragments (Figure 6b,c).

claim: AEP-derived Amphiphysin I fragments (1–278 and 279–695) promote the loss of dendritic spines in Tau P301S transgenic mice.
source: Golgi staining revealed that AEP-derived Amphiphysin I fragments (1–278 and 279–695) promoted the loss of dendritic spines in Tau P301S transgenic mice (Figure 6d,e).
evidence: Golgi staining shows decreased spine density in mice expressing fragments (Figure 6d,e).

claim: The learning ability is substantially impaired in mice expressing Amphiphysin I (1-278).
source: During the training phase, the latency to find the platform was progressively decreased in the Tau P301S transgenic mice expressing EGFP, demonstrating a learning effect. However, the learning ability was substantially impaired in mice expressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) (Figure 6f,g).
evidence: Morris water maze test shows increased escape latency in mice expressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) (Figure 6f,g).

claim: The mice expressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) show decreased time in the target quadrant in the probe trial.
source: In the probe trial, the mice expressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) showed decreased time in the target quadrant, suggesting impaired memory function (Figure 6h).
evidence: Probe trial shows decreased time in target quadrant for mice expressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) (Figure 6h).

claim: The mice expressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) have impaired memory function.
source: In the probe trial, the mice expressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) showed decreased time in the target quadrant, suggesting impaired memory function (Figure 6h).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed decrease in time spent in target quadrant.

claim: All the mice show comparable swim speeds.
source: All the mice showed comparable swim speeds (Figure 6i), suggesting that the overexpression of Amphiphysin I and its fragments does not affect motor function.
evidence: Swim speed analysis shows no difference between groups (Figure 6i).

claim: The overexpression of Amphiphysin I and its fragments does not affect motor function.
source: All the mice showed comparable swim speeds (Figure 6i), suggesting that the overexpression of Amphiphysin I and its fragments does not affect motor function.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of comparable swim speeds.

claim: The mice expressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) fragments spend less time in the new arm in the Y-maze test.
source: Consistent with the water maze test results, the mice expressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) fragments spent less time in the new arm in the Y-maze test (Figure 6j).
evidence: Y-maze test shows decreased time in new arm for mice expressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) (Figure 6j).

claim: The Amphiphysin I (1-278) fragment induces learning and memory impairments.
source: These results indicate that the Amphiphysin I (1-278) fragment induces learning and memory impairments.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from water maze and Y-maze test results.

claim: LTP of fEPSPs in the hippocampus is believed to be the basis of learning and memory.
source: The long-term potentiation (LTP) of fEPSPs in the hippocampus is believed to be the basis of learning and memory (Fedulov et al., 2007; Nicoll, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: LTP is diminished in mice overexpressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) and (279-596) fragments.
source: We found that LTP was diminished in mice overexpressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) and (279-596) fragments (Figure 6k).
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings show reduced LTP in mice expressing fragments (Figure 6k).

claim: The averaged slope of fEPSPs is smaller in mice expressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) and (279-596) fragments than in those expressing EGFP or full-length Amphiphysin I.
source: The averaged slope of fEPSPs was smaller in mice expressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) and (279-596) fragments than in those expressing EGFP or full-length Amphiphysin I (Figure 6l).
evidence: Quantification shows smaller fEPSP slope in mice expressing fragments (Figure 6l).

claim: The Amphiphysin I (1-278) and (279-596) fragments induce synaptic dysfunction in transgenic mouse models of AD.
source: Hence, the Amphiphysin I (1-278) and (279-596) fragments induce synaptic dysfunction in transgenic mouse models of AD.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing reduced synaptic density, spine loss, and impaired LTP.

claim: The density of hippocampal synapse in mice expressing AEP-uncleavable Amphiphysin I N278A mutant is much higher than that in mice expressing wild-type Amphiphysin I.
source: The density of hippocampal synapse in mice expressing AEP-uncleavable Amphiphysin I N278A mutant was much higher than that in mice expressing wild-type Amphiphysin I (Figure 7b,c).
evidence: Electron microscopy shows higher synaptic density in mice expressing N278A mutant (Figure 7b,c).

claim: Overexpression of uncleavable Amphiphysin I (N278A) decreases AT8 immunoreactivity in hippocampus sections, compared with wild-type Amphiphysin I.
source: Overexpression of uncleavable Amphiphysin I (N278A) decreased AT8 immunoreactivity in hippocampus sections, compared with wild-type Amphiphysin I (Figure 7d).
evidence: Immunostaining shows decreased AT8 in mice expressing N278A mutant (Figure 7d).

claim: Mice expressing Amphiphysin I N278A spend more time in the target quadrant in the probe test.
source: The water maze test found that mice expression Amphiphysin I N278A spent more time in the target quadrant in the probe test, indicating reversed memory function (Figure 7e).
evidence: Water maze probe trial shows increased time in target quadrant for mice expressing N278A mutant (Figure 7e).

claim: Mice expressing Amphiphysin I N278A have reversed memory function.
source: The water maze test found that mice expression Amphiphysin I N278A spent more time in the target quadrant in the probe test, indicating reversed memory function (Figure 7e).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed increase in time spent in target quadrant.

claim: The LTP is improved in mice injected with AAV-Amphiphysin I N278A compared with mice injected with AAV-wild-type Amphiphysin I.
source: The electrophysiological analysis found that the LTP was improved in mice injected with AAV-Amphiphysin I N278A compared with mice injected with AAV-wild-type Amphiphysin I (Figure 7f,g).
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings show improved LTP in mice expressing N278A mutant (Figure 7f,g).

claim: The N278A mutation which blocks the fragmentation of Amphiphysin1 reverses synaptic dysfunction and cognitive impairments in Tau P301S mice.
source: These results indicate that the N278A mutation which blocks the fragmentation of Amphiphysin1 reverses synaptic dysfunction and cognitive impairments in Tau P301S mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing improved synaptic density, reduced tau phosphorylation, improved memory, and improved LTP with N278A mutant.

claim: AEP-generated Amphiphysin I fragments are found in the AD mouse model and human AD brain.
source: In the present study, we identified a synaptic protein Amphiphysin I, which is cleaved by AEP in AD. AEP-generated Amphiphysin I fragments are found in the AD mouse model and human AD brain.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry and Western blot data from AD patients and Tau P301S mice (Figure 2d-f, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claim: The Amphiphysin I fragments disrupt clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
source: The Amphiphysin I fragments disrupt clathrin-mediated endocytosis and induce synaptic dysfunction.
evidence: This is supported by transferrin uptake and FM 4-64 labeling assays (Figure 3).

claim: Amphiphysin I fragments generated by AEP induce synaptic dysfunction and tau hyperphosphorylation, which are two of the major pathological features in the AD brain.
source: Therefore, our results indicate that Amphiphysin I fragments generated by AEP induce synaptic dysfunction and tau hyperphosphorylation, which are two of the major pathological features in the AD brain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from all the experimental results presented in the study.

claim: Amphiphysin I plays a pivotal role in clathrin-mediated endocytosis by interacting with dephosphins such as clathrin, dynamin, and Amphiphysin II.
source: Amphiphysin I plays a pivotal role in clathrin-mediated endocytosis by interacting with dephosphins such as clathrin, dynamin, and Amphiphysin II (David et al., 1996; McMahon et al., 1997; Wigge et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Amphiphysin I (1-278) fragment loses the function of binding to clathrin and dynamin.
source: We found that Amphiphysin I (1-278) fragment loses the function of binding to clathrin and dynamin, whereas the C-terminal (279-695) fragment loses the function of binding to Amphiphysin II and the cell membrane (Figures 3 and 5e).
evidence: GST pull-down assay shows loss of binding to clathrin and dynamin by (1-278) fragment (Figure 3b).

claim: The C-terminal (279-695) fragment loses the function of binding to Amphiphysin II and the cell membrane.
source: We found that Amphiphysin I (1-278) fragment loses the function of binding to clathrin and dynamin, whereas the C-terminal (279-695) fragment loses the function of binding to Amphiphysin II and the cell membrane (Figures 3 and 5e).
evidence: GST pull-down assay shows loss of binding to Amphiphysin II by (279-695) fragment (Figure 3b), and subcellular fractionation shows cytoplasmic localization (Figure 5k).

claim: During clathrin-mediated endocytosis, clathrin induces the deformation of the membrane into a budding vesicle.
source: During clathrin-mediated endocytosis, clathrin induces the deformation of the membrane into a budding vesicle (Robinson, 1994), whereas dynamin mediates the fission of the vesicle neck (Hinshaw and Schmid, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Dynamin mediates the fission of the vesicle neck during clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
source: During clathrin-mediated endocytosis, clathrin induces the deformation of the membrane into a budding vesicle (Robinson, 1994), whereas dynamin mediates the fission of the vesicle neck (Hinshaw and Schmid, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Once Amphiphysin I is cleaved, the resultant N-terminal fragment binds to the membrane and competes with full-length Amphiphysin I, which may interrupt the recruiting of clathrin and dynamin from cytosol to the endocytic site, resulting in disrupted clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
source: Once Amphiphysin I is cleaved, the resultant N-terminal fragment binds to the membrane and competes with full-length Amphiphysin I, which may interrupt the recruiting of clathrin and dynamin from cytosol to the endocytic site, resulting in disrupted clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
evidence: This is a mechanistic speculation based on the observed binding properties and functional assays.

claim: The C-terminal fragment of Amphiphysin I (279-695) recruits dynamin and clathrin but cannot help them translocate to the membrane.
source: Besides, the C-terminal fragment of Amphiphysin I (279-695) recruits dynamin and clathrin but cannot help them translocate to the membrane.
evidence: This is an inference based on the binding data and subcellular localization.

claim: Overexpression of Amphiphysin I fragments in mice induces synaptic loss, synaptic dysfunction, and memory deficits.
source: Additionally, overexpression of Amphiphysin I fragments in mice induces synaptic loss, synaptic dysfunction, and memory deficits (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy, electrophysiology, and behavioral tests (Figure 6).

claim: NFTs, which are composed of hyperphosphorylated tau, are a major characteristic of AD.
source: NFTs, which are composed of hyperphosphorylated tau, are a major characteristic of AD.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AD pathology.

claim: There is significant tau hyperphosphorylation in mice overexpressing Amphiphysin I (1-278).
source: Here, we found significant tau hyperphosphorylation in mice overexpressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) (Figure 4).
evidence: Immunostaining shows increased AT8 and AT100 in mice overexpressing Amphiphysin I (1-278) (Figure 4d).

claim: Amphiphysin I (1-278) binds to p35 with higher affinity than full-length Amphiphysin I.
source: Indeed, we found Amphiphysin I (1-278) binds to p35 with higher affinity than full-length Amphiphysin I.
evidence: His pull-down assay shows binding of Amphiphysin I (1-278) to p35 (Figure 5j).

claim: Amphiphysin I (1-278) is mainly localized in cell membranes.
source: Moreover, Amphiphysin I (1-278) is mainly localized in cell membranes, where p35 tends to be cleaved by calpain (Minegishi et al., 2010).
evidence: Subcellular fractionation shows increased Amphiphysin I (1-278) in membrane fraction (Figure 5k), and the claim about p35 cleavage is supported by citation.

claim: p35 tends to be cleaved by calpain in cell membranes.
source: Moreover, Amphiphysin I (1-278) is mainly localized in cell membranes, where p35 tends to be cleaved by calpain (Minegishi et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: More p35 is cleaved into p25 in the presence of Amphiphysin I (1-278).
source: As expected, more p35 is cleaved into p25 in the presence of Amphiphysin I (1-278).
evidence: Western blot shows increased p25 in cytoplasm fraction with Amphiphysin I (1-278) (Figure 5k).

claim: There is increased CDK5 activity in neurons overexpressing Amphiphysin I (1-278).
source: We also found increased CDK5 activity in neurons overexpression Amphiphysin I (1-278).
evidence: CDK5 activity assay shows increased histone H1 phosphorylation (Figure 5a,d,e).

claim: Inhibition of CDK5 reverses the phosphorylation of tau induced by Amphiphysin I (1-278).
source: Furthermore, inhibition of CDK5 reverses the phosphorylation of tau.
evidence: Immunostaining shows decreased AT8 and AT100 with CDK5 inhibitor treatment (Figure 5f-h).

claim: Both the in vivo and in vitro evidence indicate that Amphiphysin I (1-278) promotes the hyperphosphorylation of tau by activating CDK5.
source: Taken together, both the in vivo and in vitro evidence indicate that Amphiphysin I (1-278) promotes the hyperphosphorylation of tau by activating CDK5.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments in mice and cultured neurons.

claim: The Tau P301S mice overexpress a P301S mutant human tau that is indicated in frontotemporal dementia (FTD).
source: Here, we used the Tau P301S mice to explore the role of Amphiphysin I fragments on tau phosphorylation and synaptic dysfunction. The Tau P301S mice overexpress a P301S mutant human tau that is indicated in frontotemporal dementia (FTD).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Tau P301S mouse model.

claim: The Tau P301S mice develop tau pathology, synaptic dysfunction, and behavioral impairments.
source: Since the mice develop tau pathology, synaptic dysfunction, and behavioral impairments (Yoshiyama et al., 2007), it is widely used for the investigation of tauopathies.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The results in the present study may reflect a common mechanism in tauopathies.
source: Thus, the results in the present study may reflect a common mechanism in tauopathies.
evidence: This is a speculation about the broader applicability of the findings.

claim: Synaptic dysfunction and tau hyperphosphorylation are key pathological characteristics of AD.
source: Synaptic dysfunction and tau hyperphosphorylation are key pathological characteristics of AD.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AD pathology.

claim: The Amphiphysin I (1-278) fragment may induce synaptic dysfunction and tau phosphorylation through independent pathways.
source: As discussed above, the Amphiphysin I (1-278) fragment may induce synaptic dysfunction and tau phosphorylation through independent pathways.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed dual effects of the fragment.

claim: Amphiphysin I (1-278) causes synaptic dysfunction by interfering with clathrin-mediated endocytosis and synaptic vesicle recycling.
source: It causes synaptic dysfunction by interfering with clathrin-mediated endocytosis and synaptic vesicle recycling and enhances tau hyperphosphorylation through the p35/CDK5 pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the functional assays and mechanistic studies.

claim: Amphiphysin I (1-278) enhances tau hyperphosphorylation through the p35/CDK5 pathway.
source: It causes synaptic dysfunction by interfering with clathrin-mediated endocytosis and synaptic vesicle recycling and enhances tau hyperphosphorylation through the p35/CDK5 pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the CDK5 activity assays and p35/p25 studies.

claim: Tau hyperphosphorylation induces synaptic dysfunction.
source: However, it has been shown that tau hyperphosphorylation induces synaptic dysfunction.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous research.

claim: The hyperphosphorylated tau induced by Amphiphysin I (1-278) may also contribute to synaptic dysfunction.
source: Thus, the hyperphosphorylated tau induced by Amphiphysin I (1-278) may also contribute to synaptic dysfunction.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the known effects of hyperphosphorylated tau.

claim: Amphiphysin I is an endocytosis-related protein that plays an important role in the reuptake of neurotransmitters and the formation of synaptic vesicles.
source: Amphiphysin I is an endocytosis-related protein that plays an important role in the reuptake of neurotransmitters and the formation of synaptic vesicles.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Amphiphysin I function.

claim: The dysfunction of synaptic vesicle recycling is found in early AD and is believed to contribute to cognitive impairments.
source: The dysfunction of synaptic vesicle recycling is found in early AD and is believed to contribute to cognitive impairments (Arendt, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The dysfunction of many endocytic proteins is involved in AD, such as Amphiphysin II, CD2AP, PICALM, RIN3, and so on.
source: The dysfunction of many endocytic proteins is involved in AD, such as Amphiphysin II, CD2AP, PICALM, RIN3, and so on Karch and Goate, 2015.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Amphiphysin I fragments generated by AEP interrupt synaptic vesicle endocytosis and induce synaptic dysfunction, as indicated by impaired mEPSCs in cultured neurons and diminished LTP in brain slides expressing Amphiphysin I fragments.
source: Here, we show that Amphiphysin I fragments generated by AEP interrupt synaptic vesicle endocytosis and induce synaptic dysfunction, as indicated by impaired mEPSCs in cultured neurons and diminished LTP in brain slides expressing Amphiphysin I fragments.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data (Figure 4a-c, Figure 6k,l).

claim: Overexpression of the full-length Amphiphysin I exerts protective effects in the Tau P301S mouse.
source: In the Tau P301S mouse, overexpression of the full-length Amphiphysin I exerted protective effects, which can be explained by the beneficial effect of Amphiphysin I on synaptic function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed better outcomes with full-length Amphiphysin I compared to fragments.

claim: The protective effect of the full-length Amphiphysin I may exceed the toxic effect of the AEP-generated Amphiphysin I fragment in the experiments.
source: It is noteworthy that the overexpressed full-length Amphiphysin I could also be fragmented by endogenous AEP and generate toxic fragments. However, the protective effect of the full-length Amphiphysin I may exceed the toxic effect of the AEP-generated Amphiphysin I fragment in our experiments.
evidence: This is a speculation to explain the observed protective effects despite potential cleavage.

claim: The activity of Amphiphysin I is regulated by phosphorylation which inhibits its binding to AP-2 and clathrin.
source: The activity of Amphiphysin I is also regulated by phosphorylation which inhibits its binding to AP-2 and clathrin (Cousin and Robinson, 2001; Slepnev et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Calpain has been reported to regulate the activity of Amphiphysin I.
source: Furthermore, calpain has been reported to regulate the activity of Amphiphysin I.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous research.

claim: During neural hyperexcitation, calpain cleaves Amphiphysin I, thus inhibits synaptic vesicle recycling, which may play an auto-protective role against neural hyperexcitation.
source: During neural hyperexcitation, calpain cleaves Amphiphysin I, thus inhibits synaptic vesicle recycling, which may play an auto-protective role against neural hyperexcitation (Wu et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: AEP cleaves Amphiphysin I in an age-dependent manner.
source: Here, we found a novel posttranslational regulation of Amphiphysin I, cleavage by AEP. Noticeably, AEP cleaves Amphiphysin I in an age-dependent manner.
evidence: Western blot shows age-dependent increase in Amphiphysin I (1-278) fragment (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a-d).

claim: Overexpression of AEP-derived Amphiphysin I fragments in the AD mouse model induces synaptic dysfunction, tau hyperphosphorylation, and neurotoxicity.
source: Overexpression of AEP-derived Amphiphysin I fragments in the AD mouse model induces synaptic dysfunction, tau hyperphosphorylation, and neurotoxicity.
evidence: This is supported by multiple experiments in Tau P301S mice (Figures 4, 6).

claim: Overexpression of the Amphiphysin I mutation which is resistant to the cleavage by AEP partially reverses AD pathology.
source: Nevertheless, overexpression of the Amphiphysin I mutation which is resistant to the cleavage by AEP partially reversed AD pathology.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with N278A mutant showing improved synaptic density, reduced tau phosphorylation, and improved behavior (Figure 7).

claim: The AEP-mediated cleavage of Amphiphysin I may take part in the pathogenesis of AD.
source: Overall, our results suggest that the AEP-mediated cleavage of Amphiphysin I may take part in the pathogenesis of AD.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from all the experimental results.

claim: Blocking Amphiphysin I cleavage by AEP may be a novel therapeutic intervention for treating AD.
source: Blocking Amphiphysin I cleavage by AEP may be a novel therapeutic intervention for treating AD.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed protective effects of the uncleavable N278A mutant.
